Who are the AVLs for these types of orders 
where maybe it's high mix, but it's sustained

production or maybe it's just high volume? And, 
you know, is it always just DigiKey or Mouser?

Are you going directly to like, the semiconductor 
vendors, or the capacitor vendors, or who else?

So I think the supply chain right now 
is changing a lot. You know, basically,

when you don't have a lot of that visibility, 
you're always gonna go to the DigiKey,

the stocking distributors, let's just 
call 'em that, which is DigiKey, Mouser,

Newark. People like that where they 
just stock. Sit on it. And, you know,

the cost is gonna be a little bit more expensive 
than if you go to the supply chain distributors.

Hello, everyone. And welcome to the "Altium 
OnTrack Podcast". I'm your host, Zach Peterson.

Today, we're talking with Jay Patel, CEO of 
Amtech. I always like getting manufacturers

on here to talk about PCB design and PCB issues 
because, of course, as I've told many people,

I've made it my mission this year to learn 
as much as I can about manufacturing. So

I'm very happy to have Jay here today. 
Jay, thank you so much for being with us.
Well, thank you. I appreciate the opportunity.

Yeah, absolutely. So you are CEO 
of Amtech, which is an EMS. And

you are new on the podcast. 
So, you know, if you could,

just give us an overview of your background and 
how you got started in the electronics industry.

Yeah, so my father started the business. You 
know, he was originally, he did a few PCB fab

houses. He's a partner in them. Didn't work out 
for a couple reasons here or there. And then he

took a break from it. My mom ended up working 
at Jabil right here in Michigan. She was at the

first Madison Heights facility and then moved. 
And she kind was there when the whole thing,

you know, when Jabil really, really scaled. 
She was a solder tech and a repair tech. And

my dad always had this bug in him to start 
an electronics company. My mom knew how to

solder. I was young and cheap and available for 
work. So my dad launched the company. I mean,

I've worked, you know, I think in 95, he started 
the company. And I was in high school, college. I

worked throughout there. And then as soon as 
I was ready to come in full-time, I started,

you know, my education process stopped. I've been 
with Amtech from the beginning. So I've actually

worked on almost every single position in the 
shop floor. From soldering to testing to machine

programming to machine operation to 
optimization to inventory, MRP. Like,

I have learned everything the hard way all the 
time. So I know that process very intimately.

Yeah, that's interesting for two reasons. First, 
it kind of mirrors my, I guess, experience,

just as a child 'cause my father was a cabinet 
maker. And so I, you know, kind of grew up around

that environment and had to work every position 
in the shop. So I get that feeling. But it's also

interesting because I think a lot of companies 
in the US are, you know, as they would say,

mom and pop operations. And, you know, eventually 
kind of get passed down to the next generation.

Yeah, I think, you know, right now, 
you kind of see it with farms because,

where it goes from generation to generation. And 
it's that simple because of the capital investment

is so high to actually break into it. It's hard 
for people to kind of put the money together to

launch a manufacturing company. Once it's in the 
business, and I think manufacturing companies are

becoming that. They're kind of like, becoming 
the next version of a farm where, you know,

it stays in the family. Kids come in. They work 
there. And it's a natural transition for the kids,

if they choose to, for the kids to take over 
because they've been around it their whole lives.

So if you could, for some of our listeners 
who maybe have not ever dealt with a company

like yours, which is an EMS, could you 
tell us what is the difference between

maybe a prototyping shop or a quick-turn 
prototyper or a quick-turn assembler and

a company like yours? Is it just a matter 
of volume or is there something different?

I think there's a lot of, there's, you 
know, there's a few differences. Inherently,

it's the same thing. We're taking circuit boards 
and soldering components onto it. However,

when you wanna get a little bit more 
sophisticated and want more repeatability,

there's a lot more robust processes that 
you need to put in place. And as you scale,

you can't micromanage everything. You have 
to really get a good team going and create

the processes around that. You know, when 
you're a prototype shop, it's a one and done.

You get it in. You can have a guy. You can 
push it through. And it's pretty easy. I mean,

I'm not saying easy. Let me take that back. It's 
different than when you want repeatable results

for a particular product. The margin is less. The 
margin for error is less. The repeatability and

expectations. And people rely on your deliveries 
even more. So you need to create a really,

really good team. And when you need to have a good 
team, you need to identify where the waste and the

risks are throughout the whole process and start 
doing some Kaizen, or continuous improvement,

and Poka-Yoke the process, or implementing some 
sort of hardware or software automation so that

you can focus on what the customer wants, what 
adds value, rather than just spinning your wheels

or doing some other tactical stuff that's not 
going to be able to add value to the customer.

So there's another, I think, wrinkle there when 
we talk about maybe the difference between,

you know, quick-turn prototype shop 
and EMS. I get the one and done part

of it versus repeatability, which makes 
a lot of sense. And I think that kind of

serves the volume production customer. 
But is there a difference, in general,

between the capability you can expect at 
an EMS versus a quick-turn prototype shop?

You know, I think the shops are set 
up differently. The processes are

set up differently. And the supply chain, most 
importantly, is set up differently. When you're

a quick-turn prototype shop, you're working 
on whatever the catalog, distributors have

in stock or you've pre-bought. When 
you're doing stuff in production,

your supply chain really becomes a really, really 
important partner to you. So I think the gear

that you run out in the shop, the software 
that you have to help you set that gear up,

is different in both prototype and production 
scenarios as well as the supply chain.

So another question, I think, 
more specifically about your

company is what makes your company 
different from other EMS companies?

Yeah, so I think, you know, I always try, I always 
say this. And I don't kid myself. What I say,

you know, if I was to shut my doors, none of my 
customers would miss me in the state of Michigan,
you know, in my county, in the state of Michigan,

or globally. So what is the differentiator for 
Amtech to really exist? I think one thing is,

the biggest differentiator always comes down to 
your team. So I think our team is a phenomenal

team, which really, really created a great team 
that is customer-focused. And because of that,

we've been able to leverage our relationships 
internally and execute on them to become almost

like a quick-turn production house. So we've had 
customers come to us and say, "Hey, we're behind

on this project. We wanna launch. You know, supply 
chain and everything is saying, you know, 12 to 16

weeks. Can you do any better or even more than 
that?" And we've been able to shorten the launch

times for production from six to eight weeks. 
Another thing that we do is we try to be able,

we set up our hardware tech stack and our software 
tech stack and increase the process window. So

anything you throw at us, we can quickly launch 
without a lot of quality issues. So, you know,

some of the differentiators we have is the type of 
gear that we run. Our SMT equipment. Our software

that supports it. Our NPI processes. And one 
big thing that we have is a vapor phase reflow,

which allows us to provide the best type of 
reflow, no matter the complexity of the board

or the simplicity of the board. And we will always 
have a good solder joint. So we don't have to go

through the iterative process of creating a 
good reflow profile for that. We just throw

it in there and it just does a phenomenal 
job for us. So I think we've set ourselves

up differently in the sense that we wanna be a 
high mix, mid volume shop. And our sweet spot

is quick-turn production. Not necessarily 
quick-turn prototype. We will do quick-turn

prototype if we have a shot at the production. 
But we're not just a quick-turn proto house.

Sure, sure. Now, you've mentioned something 
a couple of times here. And I haven't asked

you about it specifically. But you've asked 
about, or you've mentioned supply chain, right?
Yeah.

And, obviously, if you're going into volume 
production, you know, the ordering process and

managing all the logistics and everything is gonna 
be a little bit different than if you're just,

you know, throwing a board at JLCPCB and, you 
know, selecting the LCSC part numbers or whatever.
Yeah.

So, clearly, there's a different approach. Can 
you dig in a little bit more on the supply chain

aspect that you deal with as an EMS versus what a 
customer might see if they're dealing with like,

a prototype house, or if they're just consigning 
components from like, the franchise distributors?

Yeah, so I think when we go into production, 
before we launch, and this is something that

we do with all of our customers, we have to do a 
complete supply chain risk analysis to see if the

parts that are in the BOM will allow us to stay 
in production for the lifecycle of the parts. And

the sooner the customers get us involved in that 
side where they're, before the BOM is locked in,

the sooner that we can identify those, the sooner 
we can provide them feedback and they can change

or up update their, either design or their AVL to 
ensure that we don't run into parts issues. Now,

once that is done, then we have to go around and 
find partners, the supply chain that say, okay,

this is our, and we have to get a commitment 
of the customer. We have to get some type of

forecast, or promise, or POs, or supply chain 
agreements with them going. So then we can go back

to our vendors and say, hey, look. We're launching 
this program. We're gonna get some safety stock.

We're gonna need visibility. We're gonna have 
to have a really, really tight relationship

with this. Let's make it happen. And then you have 
to talk to them and work with them to build that

supply chain going. So there's a lot of bonded 
inventory programs. There's a lot of programs

where they actually have inventory in-house that 
once you take it, it becomes yours. So they store,

you know, they warehouse our products that they 
own in our warehouse. So then it's quicker for

us. So there's a lot of different programs we 
have to really work with. And I think that's,

when launching those production processes, I 
think that entire step is a different mindset

that we have to make. And we have to make sure 
that we work with our vendors. I always say that,

especially electronics manufacturing, customers 
will come and go. But you're gonna be stuck with

the same distributors or you're only gonna have 
access to the same distributors. So the better

relationships you have with those distributors, 
the stronger you'll be in the long term.

I see. I see. And you mentioned the AVL, 
right? I think people would just kind of throw,

you know, DigiKey, Mouser, or Newark, 
or something like that on their AVL.

But who are the AVLs for these types 
of orders where maybe it's high mix,

but it's sustained production, or 
maybe it's just high volume and-
Yeah.

You know, is it always just DigiKey or 
Mouser? Are you going directly to like,

the semiconductor vendors, or the 
capacitor vendors, or who else?

So I think the supply chain right now is changing 
a lot. You know, basically, when you don't have

a lot of that visibility, you're always gonna 
go to the DigiKey, the stocking distributors,

let's just call them that, which is DigiKey, 
Mouser, Newark. People like that where they just

stock. Sit on it. And, you know, the cost is gonna 
be a little bit more expensive than if you go to

the supply chain distributors where they really 
focus on forecasting and creating a safety stock,

a bonded inventory program, where we're giving 
them continuous updates so they can hold that

inventory for us. So there's that tier. So 
we have our stocking distributors. We have

our supply chain distributors. And, now, what's 
happening that's really, really different is,

a lot of these OEMs, component manufacturers are 
trying to go direct. So TI is working on that.

Analog Devices is working on that. There's a lot 
of other companies that are trying to go direct.

And so the entire supply chain arena or the way 
that we integrate and work with our vendors is

changing right now because some OEMs or component 
manufacturers are deciding to sell directly. So,

now, when we're looking at different programs, we 
then also have to take into consideration that.

Because, ultimately, we need to make sure that our 
price is competitive, especially if we're trying

to focus on reshoring and onshoring product, 
which is a big push right now for us. And we've

seen a lot of interest in that. We need to make 
sure that we have the most competitive pricing

because at the end of the day, our BOM, you know, 
from 40% to 70% of the BOM is, I mean, 40% to 70%

of our cost is the BOM. So anything that we can 
save on that makes us that much more competitive.
What's driving that from the manufacturers,

right? You mentioned like, you know, Texas 
Instruments, Analog Devices, right, doing a,

you know, kind of an e-commerce model where 
you can just go onto their website and order

parts. Are they just trying to cut out 
the stocking distributors as middlemen?

So let me take a step back. I know TI does it. 
I know Microchip does it. I may have misspoke on

Analog Devices. I don't know. I'm not confirmed 
on that. So I don't wanna spread anything. But,

you know, it always comes down to, what's the 
business case? I think what they wanna do is

they wanna, you know, instead of give that margin 
to distributors, they wanna have the same price or

take, you know, one point off and save the margin 
so they're making that money internally. So I

think it all comes down to economics. And, you 
know, the big thing is, I've always seen it all

comes in circles, you know, in waves or, you know, 
a pendulum. Leadership comes in. They want to go

direct. And then another leadership comes in and 
says, "Hey, could this go indirect? It's adding

too much overhead. This may not be what we do. 
Let's go and engage with distributors again." So

I don't know if this is forever. I don't know what 
it is. But I know, right now, there are multiple

component manufacturers trying to go direct. 
And I don't know how long that's gonna last.

You know, I could also see another business 
case for that to be like, introduction of,

you know, new parts to key customers. That kind 
of thing where they can, you know, really build

that relationship and try and get companies 
to like, lock in to more and more components.

Yeah, and, you know, they've had to really do 
that. You know, I know TI has built up a good

FAE team that we work with directly on, you know, 
that our customers, we don't do design yet, but,

you know, our customers would work with 
them to, and I agree with you. You know,

ultimately, this is a relationship business that 
is long term. So the better relationships you

build with your EMS companies, your distributors, 
or even the component manufacturers, then that's

gonna drive what gets designed into the BOM. And 
that's gonna drive business. So I think, you know,

if, and that's a good point. If they want to 
own that relationship, it makes sense then.

Sure, sure. So speaking of designers, I think 
this is a good point to transition and ask you,

what are some misconceptions that design teams 
have when they start to make that transition from

prototyping to dealing with a company like 
yours that might be offering kind of this,

you know, quick production model or that might be 
producing an order at higher volume? Like produce-
So, I just-

Sorry, I just wanna bring this up, right? 
Producing at like, 20 units is way different than

producing at 20,000 units. So I wanna hear from 
you. What are the big misconceptions from designs?

Yeah, so, I mean, I don't know how long you've 
been around the industry. You can see my gray

hair. I've aged like presidents. After the supply 
chain issue, I've aged like a president. You know,

every year is like, three to four years for me. 
But I think, you know, the old guys, when the

transition was being made from surface mount, 
from through-hole to surface mount, a lot of

the engineers said, "We don't like surface mount 
because we can't iterate. I can't swap a resistor

out or I can't swap an IC out. I would like to be 
able to have that capability of doing that because

if I wanna do surface mount prototype, I have to 
get a stencil. And I have to pay for, you know,

machine setup and machine programming and 
all this kind of stuff. And it adds. I just

wanna use through-hole." And I think that is 
indicative of the same way, I mean, obviously,

we don't use through-hole anymore 'cause I 
just don't think you can get those type of

parts in through-hole. But, now, the same way 
is, I think, people, when they're prototyping,

they build it so it's ease of prototype. And 
that's okay for initial design validation builds,

engineering validation builds. That's fine. But as 
soon as you go into production, there's a lot of

things that need to be taken into account for. 
It's, you know, we need to design quality in,

remove design risks out, design automation in 
so that we can provide consistent quality and

delivery to our customers with a really, really 
simple manufacturing process that's designed for

that particular product. So I think when we take a 
step back, and, you know, we're in Detroit. We've

been lucky enough to start working with Apple 
since they started their Advanced Manufacturing

Academy over here. And one of the things that 
we really talked about is, all right, so how

can Apple help us? And I think what we started 
out with is, let's focus on creating a process

and organization that is easy for customers 
to reshore, onshore and make it confident.

And I think what we started out with, it was their 
DFM, design for manufacturability and design for

assembly rules. And Apple's actually been helping 
us design those rules that they use in their

products. And they've kind of shared that with us 
right now. So, I think, you know, even talking to

them, the first part of production success is DFM 
and DFA. And those things, we're talking about,

like, you know, what can we do? Can we make 
it single-sided or double-sided? Can we remove

the complex components? Like, do we really need a 
micro BGA on this? Like, do we really need it? Or

do we have enough room to be able to put different 
type of components that can be inspected by an AOI

or that can be swapped out if the component fails 
easily? So we try to really talk to our customers.

Like, we have a particular customer launch with 
the BGA, HDI on the boards. Takes a long time for

it to like, fabricate. And there was a drop-in 
replacement of that particular part that was a

QFN. So the next generation that's coming out 
is gonna have QFNs. That's gonna lead to a lot

of issues. Now, we're lucky enough that we have 
a vapor phase reflow. And we've been pumping out,

you know, the BGAs. No problem. But this allows 
us that flexibility that if anything does happen

and we do need to rework it, it makes life a 
lot easier to rework a QFN than it does a BGA.

There's a couple of threads I'm hearing here, 
right? You brought up DFM. But, you know,

with DFM, there's an associated, I guess, 
DFC, right? Design for cost, right? Because-
Correct.

You could design it perfectly. But it might 
be a Ferrari, right? So you followed all the

right design rules. You took account of all the 
possible assembly defects and did what you could

in the design to address it. But at the end 
of the day, it's a way overbuilt design. It's

a Ferrari. And then there's the Kia, right? 
You would love to to make it really cheap and

inexpensive. But it still does all the stuff 
that the Ferrari does, right? And so the DFM

approach is probably a little bit different there. 
And it sounds like you guys are able to maybe

identify some of those issues that could help 
reduce the cost involved, either when you're

building the Ferrari or when you're building the 
Kia. Or maybe make a Ferrari look more like a Kia.

Yeah, and I think, yeah, we have that. And the 
thing is, we do the best when our customers allow

us to engage with that process. If they just 
give us a final print and we have to build it,

well, then we'll build it. But we can add 
a lot more value to that. And, really,

we add value at no cost. You know, like, 
once you launch it, once you're a customer,

we like to be very, very tight with the 
engineering team that works on the next

generation of products when it comes for BOM 
and when it comes for layout for the circuit

boards. You know, one thing that we really push 
for and we've converted a lot of our customers is,

you know, through-hole components are still an 
issue. But at every single point when we can,

we change it so then we have pin through paste. 
We create solder preforms. So, now, you know,

those through-hole components that leads to a 
lot of defects, a lot of processing that's there,

you know, a lot of manual work, we can just get 
it done in the SMT reflow process by adding those

things. So we have that opportunity. And we take 
those type of opportunities with our customers.

And then another thread, I guess, from the 
DFM, DFA is quality control, right? And I

think this is another big misconception that 
designers might have. Because if they try to

produce the Ferrari at a quick-turn prototype 
house, the yield might be horrible, right?
Correct.

The yield might be 50%. But, you know, you, as 
the designer, don't know that. You were just happy

that you got your 10 boards back. And you don't 
care if they had to build 15 or 20 of 'em in order

to get you your 10 boards. You got your 10 boards 
and they work, right? Whereas if you're going

into an EMS, quality sounds like a lot more of an 
issue because you have that margin compression and

because you are probably trying to prevent a 
lot of that manual rework that would arise,

which then, of course, you know, eats into your 
margin and possibly adds cost to the customer.

Yeah, I mean, I think that is a very valid 
thing. And that's very important. And I think

when you're developing a product, like, you need 
to know that it's not a manufacturing defect.

Because if it's not working, you're always gonna 
default to, hey, it's a engineering defect. And,

ultimately, you lose a lot of time. You lose 
a lot of resources. You know, it becomes a

frustrating process for everybody. So even when 
we design, when the engineers design it, they

need to focus on design for manufacturability. 
And in the case that they can't, you know,

that's why we've kind of developed our hardware 
tech stack with the vapor phase reflow, our SPI,

our pick-and-place machines where 
you may have defects at Amtech,

but soldering is not gonna be a defect. 
So everything is always gonna solder well.

You know, so that's why we've kind of, you know, 
you ask, how do we differentiate ourselves? That's

one big thing, is we've widened our process 
so much that we can take anything you throw

at it. And we've done boards that are 18 to 20 
layers or more, high mass and small boards. And

it's been really a great process for us. But, you 
know, luckily, we can do that. But other EMSes,

yes, they need to get the engineers to understand 
that it has to be built and manufacturable. You

know, even, like, small little things. If you 
keep a via too close to a pad, it's gonna take

solder paste. And when it takes a solder paste, 
what happens? You can have bridging. You can

have tombstone. You know, I have an instance 
where a customer put a via under a component,

which is shorting it to ground. And that's just, 
you know, it creates all these issues. So it's

very important that the engineers go through a 
DFM process and make sure that the board is set

up so, and it's, the design is robust so that 
when you build it, it will work all the time.

Sure, sure. And then going 
back into quality control,

I think this also relates back to 
capability differences between,

you know, an EMS and a fast prototyping 
house. Maybe if you could, tell us. Is

the testing and QC processes and capabilities 
different between those two types of companies?

Yeah, I think, you know, I think there is. 
And it's changing a lot, to be honest with

you. You know, we've been implementing AI-based 
and machine learning-based visual inspection now,

which gives us, you know, it takes about, you 
know, two minutes to program. And, boom, we're

ready to go. We're inspecting products. So even if 
it's a low mix or low volume product, I'm sorry,

low volume product, we can get that. So I think 
testing in quick-turn is more visual. And, sorry,

quality control in quick-turn is more visual. And 
quality control in production is more electrical.

And so you're actually doing a functional 
test, or ICT test, or measuring components,

or measuring values on the board. And that takes a 
little bit additional firepower and sophistication

to be able to build that. You know, it really 
sucks because when you're built, not sucks,

but it's really a challenge because not only are 
you developing a product and you finally developed

that product, now, you have to create another 
product, which is a test that tests that product.

So you have double, you know, you have to increase 
your engineering effort to be able to build that

product. And a lot of companies don't like to do 
that. A lot of companies outsource that. We've

been working with a great company that helps us 
do quick-turn, turnkey, end-of-line testing. And

it's been working out for our customers. But it 
is an effort that needs to be made because at the

end of the day, you know, the test, there may be 
a capital expenditure for it and labor associated

with it. But it's still cheaper than accidentally 
sending an entire batch that doesn't work over to

the customer. And how are you gonna manage that 
line down situation? What are you gonna do? We

have to test. And we will test all product going 
out the door in a production type of environment.

So when you're dealing with clients, right, 
they send you data. And a lot of the DFM,

DFA gremlins are probably hidden somewhere 
in that data. And maybe the designer or the

customer doesn't even know about it, 
right? What are some of the common

challenges that you see when dealing 
with data as part of a customer order?

Yeah, so I always say that, you know, 
electronics is almost a trillion dollar

industry. And we have no standards on how we 
communicate our data, or how we develop our BOMs,

or how we send over PCB fabrication notes, or 
stack-ups, or anything. So every time we get

a new data package from a customer, we have to go 
through it. And it is painful because the BOM has

a different format. The mechanical information is 
a different format. The drawings have a different

format. Where's the conformal coding information 
if it's there? You know, we have to look at every

sub-note and everything to make sure that it's 
built properly. And if there is any discrepancy

in our understanding versus what the customer 
wants, it just creates a bad experience for

everybody because, you know, you have one shot to 
give, especially for new customers, you've got one

shot to lead with a good impression. And once 
you get the program and they put faith in you,

if there is a discrepancy between the understood 
scope of work and the expected scope of work,

it leads to friction. And that's not good for 
us because we wanna provide a service for our

customers. We wanna add value. We want it to be 
seamless. So, right now, it is really painful.

You know, here's a use case. Customer comes to 
us with a production order. A new production

order. We're quoting it. We quoted it. We won, 
right? We're launching. Doing NPI on it now. Now,

when the NPI happens, the board house 
really digs into the design and says,

"Okay, there's these issues on here." Now, 
if the customer is, it's a time-sensitive

launch. And the customer wants it. And we 
promise them that we'll get it to them. Now,

when we go and launch it, the board house 
comes back with EQs. And then we have to go

to the customer. And the customer says, "Well, I 
don't understand this. Why are they asking this?"

And then we go back to the board house. And that 
slows us down by two to three days. And if that-
[Zach] At least, right?

At least, yeah. At least. If that's the customer 
is engaged with us and gets us our answers right

away and if we're working with domestic board 
houses. If we're working with overseas board

houses, you know, it takes 24 to 48 hours to get 
a response for them. And then we wait for the

customer. So we're talking about a week or two, 
just going back and forth on PCB fab drawings,

and making sure we get it the right way. And 
if the board is not good, nothing you build on

top of it is gonna be good. So this is a very 
critical step in the entire process to launch

electronics. And it is not standardized. And
